Review of Last Class

Waste Allocation as a Network Problem

  • A network model’s decisions are flows; its constraints are conservation at each node.
  • Flows can be constrained and/or incur costs which influence the decision.
  • In the waste example, the WTE ran only because the landfill was full: a limit at one node set the decision at another.

Everything we have optimized so far assumed we know every number in the model. This lecture drops that assumption.

Decisions Under Uncertainty

Two-Stage Decision Problems

  • Reservoir: summer release targets are set in spring, before the summer’s inflow is known.
  • Grid: plants are committed to operate a day ahead, before wind, solar, and demand are known.

These are examples of two-stage problems with recourse: act-learn-react.

The manager has to commit to a release plan before knowing the inflow; once the inflow arrives, there is some room to adjust (cut releases, buy water elsewhere, spill), but adjustments cost something. The grid operator is the same: plants are committed a day ahead, and if the wind is lower than expected, expensive peaking plants make up the difference.

Certainty and Linear Programming

Certainty was the third assumption of linear programming (with linearity and divisibility): there is no uncertainty about the mapping from decisions to constraints and outcomes.

Common practice: solve with best estimates of parameters, then stress-test the plan using Monte Carlo to identify appropriate safety margins.

Alternative: put the uncertainty in the model, as a set of scenarios with probabilities, and optimize the expected outcome.

We relaxed divisibility with mixed integer programming; today we relax certainty. The common approach treats uncertainty after the fact: optimize for the average, then check how the plan does. The alternative builds the scenarios into the optimization itself, so the plan already accounts for having to adjust later.

Two-Stage Decisions

  1. Make a decision \(\mathbf{x}\) under uncertainty (act).
  2. Observe which scenario happens (learn).
  3. Make a recourse decision that compensates for \(\mathbf{x}\) in that scenario (react).

General Two-Stage Decision Problems

\[\max_{\mathbf{x}} \; \underbrace{f(\mathbf{x})}_{\text{first stage}} + \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\left[\underbrace{Q(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\xi})}_{\substack{\text{best recourse after} \\ \text{seeing } \boldsymbol{\xi}}}\right]\]

With discrete scenarios \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) and probabilities \(p_s\), the expectation is \(\sum_s p_s\, Q(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\xi}_s)\), or can compute with Monte Carlo.

Land Allocation Example

Land Allocation Example

A farmer has 500 acres for wheat, corn, and sugar beets. How much of each should they plant? (Birge & Louveaux, 2011)

  • Planting: $150, $230, $260 per acre.
  • Feed: 200 T wheat, 240 T corn; extra sells for $170, $150/T; buying costs 40% more.
  • Beets: $36/T up to 6,000 T, then $10/T.
  • Yields: 2.5, 3, 20 T/acre on average; ±20% in good and bad years, each with probability 1/3.

This is a classic example from Birge and Louveaux’s textbook on stochastic programming. Planting happens before the yield is known; buying and selling happen after the harvest. Beets sell for $36 a tonne up to the quota of 6,000 tonnes and $10 above it, which is less than their planting cost of $13 a tonne in an average year.

Formulation for The Average Year

\(x_i\): acres planted; \(y_i\): T bought; \(z_i\): T sold (\(z_3\) beets at the quota price, \(z_4\) above it).

\[ \begin{aligned} \max_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}} \quad & -150x_1 - 230x_2 - 260x_3 - 238y_1 - 210y_2 \\ & \quad + 170z_1 + 150z_2 + 36z_3 + 10z_4 \\ \text{subject to:} \quad & x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \leq 500 \\ & {\color{red}2.5x_1 + y_1 - z_1 \geq 200}, \qquad {\color{red}3x_2 + y_2 - z_2 \geq 240} \\ & {\color{red}z_3 + z_4 \leq 20x_3}, \qquad z_3 \leq 6000, \qquad \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \geq \mathbf{0} \end{aligned} \]

Profit is sales minus purchases minus planting. The feed constraints say what you grow plus what you buy, minus what you sell, must cover the feed. With known yields, this is an ordinary LP.

“Perfect Information” Solutions

Code 
# Two-stage farm model: one planting plan x, a copy of the purchases y and
# sales z for each scenario. With one scenario it is the ordinary LP.
# Passing `plan` fixes the planting and evaluates it; passing `min_profit`
# requires at least that profit in every scenario; `price_factors` scales the
# wheat and corn prices in each scenario. Returns the planting, the expected
# profit, and the purchases and sales in each scenario.
function farm_model(factors, probs; plan=nothing, min_profit=nothing,
                    price_factors=ones(length(factors)))
    n = length(factors)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    @variable(model, x[1:3] >= 0)             # acres planted
    @variable(model, y[1:2, 1:n] >= 0)        # T bought, per scenario
    @variable(model, z[1:4, 1:n] >= 0)        # T sold, per scenario
    if plan !== nothing
        @constraint(model, x .== plan)
    end
    @constraint(model, sum(x) <= land)
    for s in 1:n
        crop_yield = avg_yield .* factors[s]
        @constraint(model, crop_yield[1] * x[1] + y[1, s] - z[1, s] >= feed_need[1])
        @constraint(model, crop_yield[2] * x[2] + y[2, s] - z[2, s] >= feed_need[2])
        @constraint(model, z[3, s] + z[4, s] <= crop_yield[3] * x[3])
        @constraint(model, z[3, s] <= beet_quota)
    end
    # profit in each scenario: sales, minus purchases and planting
    @expression(model, profit[s in 1:n], -sum(plant_cost .* x) +
        price_factors[s] * (sell_price[1] * z[1, s] + sell_price[2] * z[2, s] -
        buy_price[1] * y[1, s] - buy_price[2] * y[2, s]) +
        beet_price * z[3, s] + beet_excess_price * z[4, s])
    if min_profit !== nothing
        @constraint(model, [s in 1:n], profit[s] >= min_profit)
    end
    @objective(model, Max, sum(probs[s] * profit[s] for s in 1:n))
    optimize!(model)
    return value.(x), objective_value(model), value.(y), value.(z)
end

# The best plan for each year type
known_plan = zeros(3, 3)
known_profit = zeros(3)
for s in 1:3
    known_plan[s, :], known_profit[s] = farm_model([yield_factor[s]], [1])
end
average_plan = known_plan[2, :]

# The two-stage plan: one planting for all three year types
stochastic_plan, stochastic_profit, stochastic_buy, stochastic_sell = farm_model(yield_factor, prob)

# Each plan's profit in each year type, with the best purchases and sales
average_plan_by_year = zeros(3)
stochastic_plan_by_year = zeros(3)
for s in 1:3
    average_plan_by_year[s] = farm_model([yield_factor[s]], [1]; plan=average_plan)[2]
    stochastic_plan_by_year[s] = farm_model([yield_factor[s]], [1]; plan=stochastic_plan)[2]
end
eev = sum(prob .* average_plan_by_year)       # average plan, judged under uncertainty
wait_and_see = sum(prob .* known_profit)      # perfect information
vss = stochastic_profit - eev
evpi = wait_and_see - stochastic_profit

# Beets the average-year plan grows above the quota in a good year [T]
good_year_excess_beets = average_plan[3] * avg_yield[3] * yield_factor[1] - beet_quota
Known year Wheat (acres) Corn (acres) Beets (acres) Profit
Average 120 80 300 $118,600
Good 183.3 66.7 250 $167,667
Bad 100 25 375 $59,950

The optimal planting decision depends on the yields for each year — which we don’t know until after planting.

What Changes About the Variables?

Variable Role
\(x_i\), acres planted fixed decision before the scenario is revealed
\(z_{ij}\), T sold quantity sold in scenario \(j\)
\(y_{ij}\), T bought quantity to buy in scenario \(j\) (recourse)

Planting happens once, so it has one copy. Buying and selling happen after the harvest, so there is a separate copy for each year type. The scenario tree lists the scenarios: one branch per scenario, with its probability. With more uncertainties or more stages, the tree branches again at each one.

The Full Two-Stage Constraints

\[ \begin{alignedat}{2} &x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \leq 500 \\[0.5ex] &\color{blue}3x_1 + y_{11} - z_{11} \geq 200, && \qquad \color{blue}3.6x_2 + y_{21} - z_{21} \geq 240 \\[0.5ex] &\color{blue}z_{31} + z_{41} \leq 24x_3, && \qquad \color{blue}z_{31} \leq 6000 \\[0.5ex] &\color{purple}2.5x_1 + y_{12} - z_{12} \geq 200, && \qquad \color{purple}3x_2 + y_{22} - z_{22} \geq 240 \\[0.5ex] &\color{purple}z_{32} + z_{42} \leq 20x_3, && \qquad \color{purple}z_{32} \leq 6000 \\[0.5ex] &\color{red}2x_1 + y_{13} - z_{13} \geq 200, && \qquad \color{red}2.4x_2 + y_{23} - z_{23} \geq 240 \\[0.5ex] &\color{red}z_{33} + z_{43} \leq 16x_3, && \qquad \color{red}z_{33} \leq 6000 \\[0.5ex] &x_i, y_{ij}, z_{ij} \geq 0 \end{alignedat} \]

Scenarios: good (blue), average (purple), bad (red).

The Two-Stage Objective

Typically to maximize expected profit:

\[\max_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}} \quad -\sum_i c_i x_i + \sum_j p_j \left(\sum_i z_{i,j} - y_{i,j}\right)\]

Other choices are possible: a quantile to hedge against bad years, or the variance of profit to smooth year-to-year swings. The appendix shows a related approach: a floor on the profit in every year type.

The expected value is one summary of performance across scenarios; it is not the only defensible one. A farmer who cannot survive a bad year might instead maximize the bad-year profit or a low quantile. That choice is a value judgment about risk, and it can change the plan.

The Stochastic Plan (Decision Under Uncertainty)

Plan Wheat (acres) Corn (acres) Beets (acres)
Average-year plan 120 80 300
Two-stage plan 170 80 250

Expected profit of the two-stage plan: $108,390.

The two-stage plan moves 50 acres from beets to wheat. Wheat on that land earns less than beets sold at the quota price, so in average and bad years the two-stage plan earns less than the average-year plan. In a good year the average-year plan grows 1,200 T of beets above the quota, which sell for only $10 a tonne, while the two-stage plan’s beets stay within the quota; there the wheat earns more.

The Two-Stage Plan (Good Year)

Crop Harvest (T) Feed (T) Bought (T) Sold (T) Price ($/T)
Wheat 510 200 0 310 170
Corn 288 240 0 48 150
Beets 6,000 6,000 36

Profit: sales $275,900 − purchases $0 − planting $108,900 = $167,000.

The planting is fixed before the yield is known; the purchases and sales are the recourse, chosen after the harvest for each year type. These are the recourse decisions the two-stage model chose for each year.

The Two-Stage Plan (Average Year)

Crop Harvest (T) Feed (T) Bought (T) Sold (T) Price ($/T)
Wheat 425 200 0 225 170
Corn 240 240 0 0 150
Beets 5,000 5,000 36

Profit: sales $218,250 − purchases $0 − planting $108,900 = $109,350.

The Two-Stage Plan (Bad Year)

Crop Harvest (T) Feed (T) Bought (T) Sold (T) Price ($/T)
Wheat 340 200 0 140 170
Corn 192 240 48 0 150
Beets 4,000 4,000 36

Profit: sales $167,800 − purchases $10,080 − planting $108,900 = $48,820.

Across the three years the profits average to the expected profit, $108,390, since each year type has probability 1/3.

Comparing Plans

Can We Compare These Numbers?

  • Average-year plan: obtained $118,600 profit
  • Two-stage plan: obtained $108,390 expected profit

Is the average-year plan better?

No. $118,600 is what that plan earns if the year is average. To compare fairly, we need to compare the expected profit across the full scenario set.

The two numbers answer different questions: one is a single-scenario profit on paper, the other is an expected value under uncertainty.

Each Plan, Year by Year

Year Average-year plan Two-stage plan
Good $148,000 $167,000
Average $118,600 $109,350
Bad $55,120 $48,820
Expected $107,240 $108,390

Value of the stochastic solution (VSS): $108,390 − $107,240 = $1,150 per year.

Board item for the VSS subtraction. Each plan is evaluated in each year with the best purchases and sales for that year. The two-stage plan earns less in average and bad years and more in a good year, where the average-year plan grows 1,200 T of beets above the quota. On balance its expected profit is higher: $108,390 against $107,240 for the average-year plan. The difference is the value of the stochastic solution: what building the uncertainty into the model is worth.

What Is a Perfect Forecast Worth?

With perfect knowledge of the upcoming year the farmer makes the best decision for that year: expected profit $115,406.

Expected value of perfect information (EVPI): $115,406 − $108,390 = $7,016 per year.

With perfect information the farmer would know the year before planting and use the best plan for it: the expected profit is the average of the three known-year profits. The gap between that and the two-stage plan is the EVPI.

Scenario Trees

Scenario Trees

Scenario trees are a useful way to map out discrete scenarios, particularly when their probabilities are chained together or conditional.

Parts of a Scenario Tree

  • The root is the here-and-now decision (planting).
  • Each branch is an outcome, with its probability.
  • Each later node holds the recourse decided there (buying and selling).
  • A path from the root to a leaf is a scenario.

Monte Carlo Scenarios

A Continuous Yield Distribution

Code 
# A normal yield factor with the same mean (1) and standard deviation as the
# three year types; as there, one factor scales all three crops' yields
yield_sd = sqrt(sum(prob .* (yield_factor .- 1) .^ 2))
yield_dist = Normal(1, yield_sd)

factor_grid = 0.4:0.01:1.6
p_dist = plot(factor_grid, pdf.(yield_dist, factor_grid), color=cb_blue,
    xlabel="Yield factor for all three crops (relative to an average year)",
    ylabel="Probability density",
    ylims=(0, 3))
vline!(p_dist, yield_factor, color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2)
for s in 1:3
    annotate!(p_dist, yield_factor[s] + 0.015, 2.8,
        text(scenarios[s], plot_font, 16, cb_vermillion, :left))
end
plot!(p_dist, size=(1200, 340), left_margin=12mm, bottom_margin=12mm)

Suppose the yield factor is normal, with the same mean (1) and standard deviation (0.16) as the three year types.

The three year types have mean 1 and standard deviation 0.2 × √(2/3) ≈ 0.16; the normal distribution keeps both, but lets the yield take any value. As in the three year types, one factor scales the wheat, corn and beet yields together.

Prices Depend on the Yield

Good harvests tend to lower prices. Suppose the wheat and corn prices, for selling and buying, are scaled by a price factor

\[g = 1 - 0.5\,(f - 1) + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.1),\]

where \(f\) is the yield factor. Beet prices are set by the contract. How many scenarios would a tree need?

With three yields and three prices for each, 9 a year, and \(9^T\) over \(T\) years.

The farmer’s yield stands in for the region’s harvest, which is what moves prices. The slope (a yield 20% above average lowers prices by 10%) and the noise from other markets are illustrative assumptions.

Sample Average Approximation

How do we find the plan with the highest expected profit?

Sample average approximation: draw \(n\) years (a yield, then a price given it), each a scenario with probability \(p_j = 1/n\):

\[\max_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}} \quad -\sum_i c_i x_i + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \left(\sum_i z_{i,j} - y_{i,j}\right)\]

There are \(n\) scenarios however many uncertainties each year has; the model needs a copy of \(\mathbf{y}\) and \(\mathbf{z}\) for each.

The constraints are the same as for the three year types, written once for each sampled year, and the wheat and corn prices in the objective are scaled by that year’s price factor.

Solving with Sampled Years

Random.seed!(1)
n_samples = 1000
price_slope = 0.5
price_noise = Normal(0, 0.1)
yield_samples = rand(yield_dist, n_samples)
# the price factor given each year's yield
price_samples = 1 .- price_slope .* (yield_samples .- 1) .+
    rand(price_noise, n_samples)
sample_prob = fill(1 / n_samples, n_samples)
sampled_plan, sampled_profit = farm_model(yield_samples, sample_prob;
    price_factors=price_samples)

Estimated expected profit: $108,961.

The Sampled Plan

Plan Wheat (acres) Corn (acres) Beets (acres)
Three year types 170 80 250
Sampled, fixed prices 141.9 84 274.1
Sampled, prices vary 140.2 84.9 275

The prices barely move the plan, but the estimated expected profit falls from $110,272 to $108,961: more grain is sold when prices are low, and corn is bought when they are high.

The sampled plans grow more beets and less wheat. With three year types, beets beyond 250 acres go over the quota in the good year, one year in three. With yields that can take any value, the plan’s 275 acres of beets go over the quota only when the yield factor is above 1.09, in about 29% of years. The estimates are expected profits under the sampled distribution, so they aren’t comparable with the $108,390 from three year types.

Key Takeaways

Key Takeaways

  • The plan that is optimal for the average year need not be optimal in expectation.
  • Two stages: one here-and-now decision, one recourse decision per scenario, weighted by probability.
  • Compare plans under uncertainty: VSS is what modeling uncertainty is worth; EVPI, what a perfect forecast is worth.
  • A scenario tree lays out the scenarios: each path from the root to a leaf is one, and its probability is the product of the branch probabilities along it.

Appendix

“Risk-Averse” Optimization

The two-stage plan earns $48,820 in a bad year. What if the farmer needs a profit of at least \(F\) in every year?

Keep expected profit as the objective, and add a constraint for each scenario \(j\):

\[ \begin{aligned} & -150x_1 - 230x_2 - 260x_3 - 238y_{1,j} - 210y_{2,j} \\ & \quad + 170z_{1,j} + 150z_{2,j} + 36z_{3,j} + 10z_{4,j} \geq F \end{aligned} \]

The left side is the profit in scenario \(j\). A lower yield never raises a fixed plan’s profit, so the bad-year constraint is the one that binds. The farmer chooses \(F\): the profit they need to get through a bad year. In the code, farm_model adds these constraints when it is given min_profit.

How Much Does This Risk Aversion Cost?

Code 
# The best plan for floors from below the two-stage plan's bad-year profit up to
# the highest floor any plan can meet: the best profit in a known bad year
floors = range(45000, known_profit[3]; length=60)
floor_plan = zeros(length(floors), 3)
floor_profit = zeros(length(floors))
for k in 1:length(floors)
    floor_plan[k, :], floor_profit[k] = farm_model(yield_factor, prob; min_profit=floors[k])
end

# The plans in the table on the next slide
table_floors = [52000, 56000, known_profit[3]]
n_rows = length(table_floors) + 1
table_plan = zeros(n_rows, 3)
table_expected = zeros(n_rows)
table_plan[1, :] = stochastic_plan
table_expected[1] = stochastic_profit
for k in 1:length(table_floors)
    table_plan[k + 1, :], table_expected[k + 1] =
        farm_model(yield_factor, prob; min_profit=table_floors[k])
end

p_floor = plot(floors ./ 1000, floor_profit ./ 1000, color=cb_blue,
    xlabel="Floor on profit in every year  [\$1000]", ylabel="Expected profit  [\$1000]",
    ylims=(80, 115))
scatter!(p_floor, table_floors ./ 1000, table_expected[2:end] ./ 1000, color=:black,
    markersize=7)
# below the two-stage plan's bad-year profit, the floor doesn't bind
vline!(p_floor, [stochastic_plan_by_year[3] / 1000], color=:black, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2)
annotate!(p_floor, stochastic_plan_by_year[3] / 1000 + 0.2, 84,
    text("two-stage plan's\nbad-year profit", plot_font, 16, :left))
plot!(p_floor, size=(1200, 340), left_margin=12mm, top_margin=6mm)

A floor of $56,000 costs $1,144 of expected profit; raising it to $59,950 costs $20,646 more.

Below $48,820 the two-stage plan already meets the floor, so nothing changes. The curve bends where the wheat is down to 100 acres, just enough for the feed in a bad year; above that, the beets can only take land from corn, and the cost rises steeply.

Plans with Varying Floors

Floor Wheat (acres) Corn (acres) Beets (acres) Good year Expected
None 170 80 250 $167,000 $108,390
$52,000 138.1 100 261.9 $161,476 $107,976
$56,000 106.3 100 293.7 $149,413 $107,246
$59,950 100 25 375 $113,250 $86,600

Higher floors move land from wheat to beets. In a bad year an acre of beets earns $316 above its planting cost, and an acre of wheat beyond the feed $190. In a good year, beets beyond 250 acres go over the quota and sell for $10/T. The highest floor, $59,950, is the most any plan can earn in a bad year; the plan that meets it is the best plan for a known bad year.

How Many Samples?

Code 
# Estimated expected profit from 20 independent sets of samples of each size
sample_sizes = [10, 30, 100, 300, 1000]
n_sets = 20
estimates = zeros(length(sample_sizes), n_sets)
beet_acres = zeros(length(sample_sizes), n_sets)
for k in 1:length(sample_sizes)
    m = sample_sizes[k]
    for r in 1:n_sets
        samples = rand(yield_dist, m)
        prices = 1 .- price_slope .* (samples .- 1) .+ rand(price_noise, m)
        plan, estimates[k, r] = farm_model(samples, fill(1 / m, m);
            price_factors=prices)
        beet_acres[k, r] = plan[3]
    end
end

p_sizes = plot(xscale=:log10, xticks=(sample_sizes, string.(sample_sizes)),
    xlabel="Number of sampled years", ylabel="Estimated profit  [\$1000]",
    xlims=(7, 1400))
for k in 1:length(sample_sizes)
    scatter!(p_sizes, fill(sample_sizes[k], n_sets), estimates[k, :] ./ 1000,
        color=cb_blue, markersize=7, markerstrokewidth=0, alpha=0.5)
end
plot!(p_sizes, size=(1200, 340), left_margin=12mm, top_margin=6mm)

Each estimate is a Monte Carlo average over \(n\) sampled years, so the spread shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{n}\).

Each column is 20 independent sets of samples. The standard deviation of the 20 estimates falls from $13,288 with 10 samples to $1,200 with 1,000. The plans settle too: with 1,000 samples, the beets range from 274.2 to 280.6 acres across the 20 sets.
